cards.front: Effective Java Item 42 — why prefer a lambda to an anonymous class?
cards.back: It says the same thing in far less code, and the compiler reads the target type from context
cards.extra: An anonymous class repeats the interface name, the method signature and the braces. A lambda keeps only the body — same semantics, less noise.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::05 Functional Programming::01 Functional Interfaces

cards.front: Effective Java Item 43 — when is a method reference better than a lambda?
cards.back: When the lambda only calls an existing method — String::length instead of s -> s.length()
cards.extra: Short and named. Use a lambda when you need to pass arguments or do anything beyond forwarding.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::05 Functional Programming::01 Functional Interfaces

cards.front: Effective Java Item 44 — what should you use instead of defining your own functional interface?
cards.extra: Standard interfaces give you default methods (andThen, compose) and interoperability. Write your own only when the contract differs meaningfully.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::05 Functional Programming::01 Functional Interfaces

cards.front: Effective Java Item 45 — what is the risk of rewriting every loop as a stream?
cards.back: Streams are a paradigm, not just an API — forcing them into everything makes code harder to read and can be slower
cards.extra: The book's advice: use streams where they express the computation, loops where they do not, and measure rather than assume.

cards.front: Effective Java Item 46 — why must functions passed to streams be side-effect-free?
cards.back: The stream may reorder, parallelise or skip work; side effects make results depend on execution order
cards.extra: Accumulating into an external list with forEach is the classic mistake. Use collect and let the collector do it.

cards.front: Effective Java Item 47 — what should a method return when it produces a sequence?
cards.back: A Collection where possible — it is iterable and offers the Collection API
cards.extra: Returning Stream forces callers to adapt; returning Collection gives both. Only return a Stream when laziness or infinite size matters.

cards.front: Effective Java Item 48 — when is a parallel stream a bad idea?
cards.back: With blocking I/O, small data, ordered results, or shared mutable state
cards.extra: Parallelism only pays for CPU-bound, independent, easily splittable work. Otherwise it adds overhead and bugs — and the common ForkJoinPool is shared with everything else.

cards.front: Effective Java Item 49 — what should a method do with an invalid argument?
cards.back: Fail fast: validate at the start and throw an unchecked exception such as IllegalArgumentException
cards.extra: Catching it early produces a clear stack trace at the call site instead of an obscure failure later inside the method.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::02 Attributes and Methods

cards.front: Effective Java Item 50 — what is a defensive copy and when is it required?
cards.back: Copying a mutable object on the way in and out so callers cannot change your state
cards.extra: A Date passed to a constructor and stored directly lets the caller mutate your field afterwards. Copy if the class promises immutability.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::02 Attributes and Methods

cards.front: Effective Java Item 51 — what is wrong with a method that takes a boolean parameter?
cards.back: The call site reads foo(true) with no idea what true means
cards.extra: Prefer an enum or two well-named methods. The same applies to long parameter lists: split into a builder or an object.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::02 Attributes and Methods

cards.front: Effective Java Item 52 — why is overloading dangerous when the overloads take different subtypes?
cards.back: Overload selection happens at compile time, based on the static type
cards.extra: Passing a Set into classify(Set)/classify(List) can pick a different method than you expect. The book's advice: avoid ambiguous overload sets.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::02 Attributes and Methods

cards.front: Effective Java Item 53 — what does a varargs method cost at the call site?
cards.back: An array allocation per call, even for zero arguments
cards.extra: Use varargs for genuinely variable argument counts. When you need at least one, take one ordinary parameter before the varargs.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::02 Attributes and Methods

cards.front: Effective Java Item 54 — why return an empty collection instead of null?
cards.back: Every caller would otherwise need a null check; an empty collection iterates and behaves normally
cards.extra: Returning null pushes a bug into every call site. Return Collections.emptyList() instead.

cards.front: Effective Java Item 55 — when should a method return Optional?
cards.back: When it may legitimately have no result and the caller must decide what to do
cards.extra: Never return null for an Optional, never use it for collections, and do not wrap primitives — OptionalInt exists for that.

cards.front: Effective Java Item 56 — what must every exposed API element have?
cards.back: A doc comment stating the contract: what it does, preconditions and postconditions, plus @param/@return/@throws
cards.extra: The doc comment is the contract; the code is one implementation of it. Undocumented public API is unfinished API.
